:::{#thm-normal-density-max}
#### The maximum of the normal density

If $X \sim \ndist{\mean, \ss}$ ([normal distribution](random-variables.qmd#def-normal)),
then its density is largest at $x = \mean$,
where it equals:

$$\max_x \p(X=x) = \frac{1}{\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}}$$

:::

::: proof

For every real $x$, the exponent in the density is at most $0$:

$$
\ba
-\frac{(x-\mean)^2}{2\ss}
&\le 0
&& \text{(a square is non-negative, and } 2\ss > 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

The exponential function is increasing,
so the exponential factor is at most $1$,
with equality only when the exponent is $0$:

$$
\ba
\ef{-\frac{(x-\mean)^2}{2\ss}}
&\le \ef{0}
&& \text{(the exponential function is increasing)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(} \text{e}^0 = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

The exponent is $0$ exactly when $x = \mean$.
Multiplying by the positive constant $1 / (\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi})$ preserves the inequality:

$$
\ba
\p(X=x)
&= \frac{1}{\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}} \ef{-\frac{(x-\mean)^2}{2\ss}}
&& \text{(normal density)} \\
&\le \frac{1}{\sdpar\sqrt{2\pi}}
&& \text{(the exponential factor is at most } 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

Equality holds at $x = \mean$, so that value is the maximum.

:::
